blocks.md:
Credit means borrowing money now and paying it back later. A lender trusts you to pay it back.

When you use a credit card, you're not spending your own money. You're borrowing the bank's money. You have to pay it back, and often with **interest**, which is the cost of borrowing.

**Why credit matters**
Lenders look at how you've handled credit before. Good credit can help you:
• Get a car loan or home loan
• Pay lower interest rates
• Rent an apartment more easily
• Sometimes, get cheaper insurance

**Credit is a tool**
Used well, it builds trust and saves money. Used badly, it leads to debt that's hard to escape.

A credit score is a number that shows how likely you are to pay back money. The most common one is the **FICO score**. It runs from 300 to 850. Higher is better.

**What goes into a FICO score**
• **Payment history (about 35%):** Do you pay on time?
• **Amounts owed (about 30%):** How much of your credit are you using?
• **Length of history (about 15%):** How long have you had credit?
• **New credit (about 10%):** Have you opened lots of new accounts lately?
• **Credit mix (about 10%):** Do you have different kinds of credit?

**The big lesson**
Paying on time matters most. One late payment can hurt your score for years.
**Remember:** You don't need a credit card to start learning. Understanding these five parts now puts you ahead.

question.prompt: What has the biggest effect on a FICO credit score?
question.hint: Lenders care most about whether you pay them back.
question.explanation: Payment history is about 35% of a FICO score. Paying on time matters most.

blocks.md:
Your credit report is the record behind your score. It lists your accounts, balances, payments and any problems.

Three big companies keep credit reports in the US: **Equifax, Experian and TransUnion**. Each may have slightly different information.

**Check it for free**
You can get free credit reports from all three at **AnnualCreditReport.com**. That's the official site. Watch out for look-alike sites that try to charge you.

**What to look for**
• Accounts you don't recognize
• Late payments that weren't late
• Wrong names or addresses

If something is wrong, you can dispute it with the credit bureau. Errors happen, and fixing them can raise your score.
**Parent tip:** Kids usually shouldn't have a credit report at all. If yours does, it could be a sign of identity theft. You can check and freeze a child's credit with each bureau.

modules.discussionPrompt: What's a safe first step to start building credit?

widget.intro: Set a card limit and a balance. See how much of your credit you're using.

blocks.md:
Everyone starts with no credit. Here are safe ways to begin.

**Become an authorized user**
A parent can add you to their card. Their good habits can help your credit. Make sure their history is strong first.

**Get a secured card**
You put down a deposit, often a few hundred dollars. That becomes your limit. Use it for small buys and pay it off each month.

**Try a student card**
These are made for people new to credit. Limits are usually low.

**Know the age rules**
In the US, you must be 18 to get your own card. If you're under 21, you also need to show you can pay on your own, usually with your own income.

**Start small**
Put one small bill, like a streaming plan, on the card. Then pay it in full every month.

items.title: Using a card the smart way

blocks.md:
A credit card can help you build credit or trap you in debt. These habits keep you safe.

**Pay the full balance every month**
If you pay in full by the due date, you usually pay **no interest** on purchases. That's called the grace period.

**Turn on autopay**
Set it for at least the minimum so you're never late. Then pay the rest yourself.

**Keep your balance low**
Your credit utilization is your balance divided by your limit. Many experts suggest staying under 30%. Under 10% is even better.

**Only buy what you could pay in cash**
If you couldn't afford it today, a card doesn't change that.

**Watch the APR**
Card interest rates are often high. Carrying a balance can make a $100 purchase cost much more.
**Minimum payment trap:** Paying only the minimum keeps you in debt for a long time and costs much more in interest.

blocks.md:
If you owe money on cards, you're not alone. Here's a plan.

**1. Stop adding to it**
Put the card away while you pay it down.

**2. List every debt**
Write the balance, interest rate and minimum payment for each.

**3. Pick a method**
• **Avalanche:** Pay extra on the highest interest rate first. This saves the most money.
• **Snowball:** Pay extra on the smallest balance first. Quick wins keep you motivated.

Both work. The best one is the one you'll stick with.

**4. Call your lender**
Ask for a lower rate or a payment plan. It doesn't hurt to ask.

**5. Avoid quick fixes**
Payday loans and "debt relief" offers with big fees often make things worse.
